# A window is not the whole room
## Opening problem
The fictional Bellweather studio tests ceramic tiles. Inspectors used to check only the tiles nearest the kiln door. Those tiles were easy to reach, but the studio found that they did not represent the back shelves.
## Sampling rule
The revised plan divides the kiln into front, middle and back zones. An inspector takes two tiles from each zone before deciding whether the batch needs another inspection. The same pattern is repeated for every batch.
## Observations
Front tiles looked smooth in the first trial. Several back tiles had rough edges. The notes record appearance only, not the cause of the roughness.
## Avoiding a shortcut
Picking six convenient tiles from the front is not equivalent to taking two from each zone. Equal total counts do not fix a plan that omits a whole part of the kiln.
## Interpretation
A visible sample can give a distorted picture of a larger collection. The selection plan matters, not just the number of objects inspected. A balanced check makes the less convenient zones visible.
## Limits
This is a fictional teaching demonstration. It does not establish that zone causes roughness. The notes give no author, chemical composition, firing temperature or numerical defect rate.

## Record 1: inspection log
The team labels front, middle and back trays before collection. In this demonstration record 1, the two middle tiles are placed in a separate envelope. Labels make the origin of each observation visible. The envelope is a record-keeping device; it does not prove why any surface changed. Inspection still uses the three-zone rule. The record describes procedure rather than a final quality verdict.

## Closing conclusion
The central lesson is representative observation: deliberately look beyond the easiest window before drawing a conclusion about the whole collection. The speaker calls this the widen-the-window principle. The presentation offers no causal account of the rough edges.

documents.name: Tide relay.md
documents.text:
# Tide relay
A fictional harbor team sends a status flag after each stage. Mina records a reading, Oren checks the record, and Lio posts the approved flag. Posting waits for the check; recording alone never authorizes it.
## Lesson
The stages separate observation, checking and communication. The signal should reflect a checked record rather than the first impression. A stage's output becomes the next stage's input.
## Unstated details
The notes do not give the flag's color, a real harbor location, or the time of day.

# Travel kit

documents.name: Tea and shadows.md
documents.text:
# Tea and shadows
In an original fictional story, Neri invites a new neighbor for tea. The neighbor says little, then returns the next day with a repaired cup. Neri places two cups on the table without asking for an explanation.
## Narration
The narrator describes the repeated invitation and the repaired cup, but never states the neighbor's thoughts. The final scene repeats the two-cup image from the opening.
